beats.lead: The story everyone half-remembers about zero.
beats.text: Medieval Europe feared it as the Devil's numeral, and the Church banned it outright.
beats.note: It's in bestselling books. One calls zero 'contraband.' Another says merchants used it in secret, supposedly why the English word for a secret code is cipher.

beats.lead: One historian actually traced this back to its sources.
beats.text: Oxford's C. Philipp Nothaft found no medieval document that calls zero satanic, and no Church ban on record at all.
beats.note: The trail leads back to a single 1905 article by a philologist, expanded by popular writers from the late 1980s onward.

beats.name: Arte del Cambio, Florence
beats.role: The city's money-changers' guild, whose surviving statute really does bar members from writing account entries in Hindu-Arabic figures, ordering plain written-out letters instead.

beats.lead: Here's the part usually bolted on afterward.
beats.text: That a 0 could be forged into a 6 or a 9, the reason given in most retellings.
beats.note: The guild's actual 1299 text never says this. It gives no reason at all. The forgery explanation was added by a modern author, in the year 2000.

beats.text: Even the word cipher isn't a clue. It's just Arabic sifr, zero, spelled the Latin way.

beats.line: No satanic ban. Just bankers who wanted plain writing.
